objectives: Students will be able to identify the reported infiltration rate, location, date, and measurement context in each East Lawn study.
Students will be able to compare the two reports and describe how their findings agree and differ.
Students will be able to explain why the conflicting field-test results do not establish either reported rate as definitive.
Students will be able to assess method differences and measurement error as possible explanations for the conflicting results without treating either explanation as confirmed.
Students will be able to recommend relevant evidence and retesting steps for investigating the conflicting measurements.
Students will be able to decide whether the reported infiltration rate is sufficiently established to support approval of a rain-garden design.

plan.title: Interpreting the conflicting East Lawn results
plan.instructions: Create exactly two first-year-level multiple-choice questions using both sources: East Lawn Study A (east-lawn-study-a.pdf), which reports 50 mm/hour, and East Lawn Study B (east-lawn-study-b.pdf), which reports 5 mm/hour for East Lawn on 15 September 2025. Do not present either rate as settled fact. Ask learners to interpret what the discrepancy means and what records, checks, or comparable retesting could help evaluate or reconcile the results. Explain that the conflicting preliminary field-test reports leave the infiltration rate uncertain; neither report alone establishes which rate is correct. Cite both studies in the question feedback or explanation. Do not add questions beyond these two.

questions.text: East Lawn Study A reports 50 mm/hour and East Lawn Study B reports 5 mm/hour for East Lawn on 15 September 2025. Which statement best describes what these figures establish?
questions.explanation: East Lawn Study A reports 50 mm/hour from a field test and describes its result as preliminary. East Lawn Study B reports 5 mm/hour from a field test at the same location and date. Their conflicting reports are evidence, but neither alone establishes the correct infiltration rate. The sources do not support treating either value as definitive or using their average as the established rate.

sourceReferences.excerpt:
East Lawn Study B

Study B reports an infiltration rate of 5 millimetres per hour at East Lawn on 15 September 2025,
based on a field test.

This conflicts with Study A at the same location and date. The discrepancy may reflect method or
measurement error; both reports need reconciliation.

East Lawn Study A

Study A reports an infiltration rate of 50 millimetres per hour at East Lawn on 15 September 2025,
based on a field test.

This suggests East Lawn may accept runoff quickly. The result is preliminary and should be checked
before a rain-garden design is approved.

questions.text: East Lawn Study A reports 50 mm/hour, while East Lawn Study B reports 5 mm/hour for a field test at the same location on 15 September 2025. What does this disagreement allow you to conclude about the infiltration rate?
questions.explanation: East Lawn Study A reports 50 mm/hour, while East Lawn Study B reports 5 mm/hour for the same location and date. These conflicting preliminary field-test results leave the infiltration rate uncertain; neither report alone establishes which estimate is correct. Checking the methods and records or conducting comparable retesting could help evaluate the discrepancy. A plausible runoff implication or a conservative planning choice does not establish which measurement is accurate, and averaging the reports does not reconcile their disagreement.
